project.text:
**The spontaneity of the Lord: the self-aware light**

This is where the whole Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī begins — with the spontaneity, the
svācchandya, of the Lord. And the doctrine is announced in its fullness from the first lines. The blue
and the yellow and the jar are not things that a light shines upon from outside; they shine forth
*as* the light, without abandoning their own being, and are one with the manifestation itself. This —
that the world shines as the consciousness, and that the consciousness shines as the world — is the
Lord's spontaneity.

The Lord is of the nature of consciousness. He shines forth as the whole variety of knowers and knowns,
with a body that appears as if it were more than consciousness even though it is not more; and — this is
decisive — he is *aware* of shining. The image Abhinavagupta uses is the mirror. A mirror reflects the
wall, the house, the elephant, the horse, the person, the pot, the potter — all the distinctions of
part and whole, support and supported, cause and effect — without being more than its own smooth
surface. But the mirror does not know that it reflects. That is its only limit; it is inert. The Lord
is the mirror that *knows*: he shines forth as all things, and he is aware that he does so, because
consciousness culminates in reflexive-awareness. The light that shines is the light that knows itself
shining.

And this answers the obvious objection: "then it would always shine." For the "always" has no
independent time against which it could fail. What we call time is just the sun's movement — the
shining of things in their succession. To ask "why does the world shine as the sun moves?" is like
asking "why does the blue not shine as yellow?" It is the nature of the light to shine; there is no
time outside it that could make it shine or not. So the Lord is: *śaśvat*, un-cut by time; *acchanna*,
never becoming other than his own form; *svaccha*, clear — able to appear as more than himself while
being only

project.text:
**The homage that is two-resting, and who is worthy to make it**

The work opens with a prostration — and Abhinavagupta takes care to say what that prostration is. It
is not a bending of the body, nor an empty sound. It is a *two-resting* homage: it rests at once in the
Lord, whom it exalts, and in the devotee, whom it subordinates. The words of homage — "jaya," "victory,"
"namaḥ," "I bow," "I worship" — all move by one of these two directions, but each must culminate in the
other. The "victory" of the Lord, to be real, requires the devotee's self-subordination; the "I bow" of
the devotee, to be real, must rest in the Lord's excess. The two — the exalting and the subordinating —
are one act, two aspects, made manifest by the single word of homage before the whole assembly.

And the attaining of the Lord, the commentary tells us, is the attainment of *dāsya* — of
servant-ness. And the servant-ness is extremely hard to get: that is what "kathaṃcit," "in some way,"
means. It is not a title; it is the very heart of the eligibility. And it is fruitful of the greatest
good — for in becoming the servant of the Lord one attains the Lord's own excess, and all the fortunes
(dāsyalakṣmī) follow from that servant-ness, granted by the Lord's grace. It is this that makes the
devotee one who has attained all.

The homage, moreover, is made in the mind and the speech — the mind-awareness and the word-essence —
never in the inert body. "Even by speech," the text says, and by the "even" we understand "and by the
body." But the prostration proper is the offering of the undivided mind-and-speech, which is the
consciousness-power itself; and in offering that, the devotee offers the whole world to the Lord. As the
teaching says: "he should offer his own self." The physical prostration — the bowing, the eight-limbed
salutation — is only the upacāra, the visible mark by which the inner offering is inferred, not the
primary act.

And so the question of who is worthy. The objection arises: "

project.text:
**The own-self: the one consciousness, whose body is the world**

The kārikā says that the own-self alone is the Lord. But what is this "own-self"? Does it reach the
whole world — the inert things, the void, everything? The objector presses hard on this. If the
maheśvara is the self of the blue, then he must be the self of the yellow too; and then how can the
world be divided — "this is the blue, this is the yellow"? The answer turns on what "own-self" really
means.

The "own" in "own-self" (svātmā) is not restricted to anything in particular; so it is the self's own —
the inner, non-other-dependent, un-conditioned relation. And what is that? It is consciousness. For
the conscious things, he is plainly the one self. But for the inert — the lump of clay, the blue — how
can they have one self, since separate things seem to have separate natures? Here Abhinavagupta shows
that the inert, in its supposed inertia, has no real being at all. If the clay is truly in itself, is
it or is it not? If it were not, nothing would suffer; if it did its effect, so what; if it shone,
what is its own glory? The "it shines for me, for Caitra" fails too — for the perception belongs to
the perceiver, not to the thing; and "by the perceiver it shines" is a new-fangled reason that would
make the white make the yellow white. In truth, the thing has no being apart from its being-manifested;
and being-manifested is the consciousness's own act. So the blue and the yellow are not things with
their own separate bodies; they are *awareness-forms* (bodhātmānaḥ) — and their own-self, no less than
ours, is the maheśvara.

What of the void, the mere nothing? If it is cognized at all, then the maheśvara is its self too; if
it is not cognized, then it is nothing, and no one's self is at issue. The test is always the same: is
it cognized? That is the whole answer — the "being-cognized" is what makes anything the self of the
one consciousness.

project.text:
**The eternal knower: "I was never not"**

Memory seems to bind the self to the past — to what the self has itself experienced. But then the
objection arises, and it is a sharp one. "I was not at the time of the Rāmāyaṇa," the reader says.
"Vālmīki composed it long ago, and I was not there to experience it; so how can the self, which
remembers only what it has experienced, be the eternal knower?"

Abhinavagupta answers that the objection mistakes the body for the self. It is true that *this body*
was not at the time of the Rāmāyaṇa — but that is not the self. The "I"-recollection, the aham-vimarśa,
is of the consciousness-nature, and it is eternal. And here is the crucial move: if memory reaches only
what has been experienced, then even the Vālmīki of the Rāmāyaṇa was an experiencer; and the āgama
itself, by which we learn of that time, presupposes an experiencer. What flashes in the "we were not" —
the past-time-appearance, in the perfect tense — is itself a cognition; and since it is not the
experience-form (else the past would flash like the yogin's present), it must be memory. And memory, by
its very nature, presupposes a prior experience. So every memory, even the memory of the Rāmāyaṇa, points
back to an experiencer who was there.

This is where the eternal knower enters. The pure consciousness-mere, being free of the tint of time,
cannot by itself bear the memory; the memory is of the body-and-the-rest-tinted. But the tint of the
prior body is distinct from the tint of this body — so the memory-ness, if pinned to the body, would not
be clear (as the young man who was never a child would have no clear memory of childhood). The clear
memory requires the firm conceit of the experiencer — and that conceit, in its root, is the self that
was there. And that self, being consciousness, is not cut by time.

So the manifestation of the self is not un-precedented (apūrva). It does not begin to shine at some
moment; it was always shining. The being-ness of the self rests

project.text:
**The self is the Lord: what the recognition does**

The kārikā declares that the self alone is the Lord. And at once a sharp objection arises. A valid
means of knowledge, it is said, establishes what was *not* established before — it serves the practical
dealings of the world. But the Lord-self, on our own showing, is already established. So what could a
pramāṇa possibly do here? What is there left for it to prove?

Abhinavagupta's answer turns this objection around. For an inert object, even an established one, the
pramāṇa does indeed make a new attainment — it brings out some part that was not yet grasped, at least
the manifestation and the designation (prakhyā and upākhyā) of the thing in our dealing with it. But in
the self — the Lord — there is nothing un-attained to be established. The manifestation and the
designation are already there; without them, not even a trace of a thing could be known at all. So the
pramāṇa here is not establishing something new.

What, then, is it doing? It is *foregrounding* what is already present but hidden. The recognition
(pratyabhijñā) does not bring the Lord into being; it brings the Lord, who was always near and always
present, into the *foreground of our own awareness*. As Abhinavagupta says, what is hidden and standing
close by is shown as primary, by the coming-together of the heart. The recognition makes the
manifestation and the designation of the self-as-Lord no longer an instrument lost among the things of
the body and the world, but the primary thing that we see. It is the turning of the attention — the
"see, see" — upon what was always before us.

And this recognition is the very content of the whole teaching. After the upoddhāta, the opening, the
whole śāstra that is to come has, as its to-be-said content, the recognition — which is the
jñāna-kriyā, the knowledge-and-action power, made firm by the conviction (dṛḍhaniścaya) that arises from
it. The two powers — knowledge and action — are determined at length through

project.text:
**The self is the Lord: against the Buddhist no-self**

The upoddhāta, the preliminary of the whole work, must first clear the ground — by showing who denies
the self's lordship and why their denial fails. Not everyone is a real opponent. The materialist, the
Cārvāka, cannot even argue: having no means of proof of their own, they cannot refute the other side
without first adopting the very conventions of proof they reject. The Sāṃkhya, with its many selves or
its one self with hidden lordship, is not wholly far from us. The real opponent — the one who must be
met head-on — is the **Buddhist**, the Sautrāntika, who denies the self outright. It is his no-self that
the eleven verses of this vimarśa set out and answer.

The Buddhist's attack is twofold. First, he denies the self that we claim to perceive: "the self is
not seen," he says, "only the momentary cognitions flash by, with their own-mark appearances." Second,
he denies the self that we might infer: memory and the synthesis, he holds, are otherwise established —
they are only the work of the impressions in the stream, with no abiding owner behind them. So the
self, whether taken as perceived or as inferred, is rejected; and with it, he concludes, the whole
apparatus of the knowledge-action relation — the very lordship we ascribe to the self — collapses, for
there is no one to be the knower and the doer.

Abhinavagupta meets him on both fronts. To the denial of the perceived self, he answers with the
"I"-cognition itself (ahaṃpratyaya): the self is not some object hidden behind the perceptions — it is
present, unmistakably, in the very act of saying "I." The "I" is not a thing seen among others; it is
the seeing itself, that which is present in every cognition, never itself absent. The ādi — the stream
of the senses, the breath, the knowledge — all presuppose this "I" that runs through them. The Buddhist's
"the self is not seen" fails: the self is the seer, and the seer is never not seen, for he is the
seeing.

project.text:
**The cognition cannot be a thing: the dilemma of the consciousness-form**

The Buddhist had denied the self. But he had also, in a different mood, offered a reason for the
self's lordship — "by the union of knowledge and action." To stop even this, Abhinavagupta turns the
same logic against the cognition itself. Whatever the opponent says cognition is, it cannot stand.
And he forces the choice with a single dilemma, put in the seventh kārikā: if the cognition is of the
consciousness-form, then it must be eternal, like the self; but if it is inert, then it cannot reveal
any object at all. There is no third option.

Take the first horn. The consciousness-nature is, by its very marker, *self-manifestation* — it is the
light that knows itself. And self-manifestation is directly opposed to being-an-object, to being
manifested by another. A thing that is manifest by another is caught in place and time — it is here or
there, now or then. But the self-manifest light is free of all such being-caught. If the cognition were
truly of the consciousness-form, it could not be the momentary, place-and-time-bound thing the Buddhist
takes it to be; it would have to be eternal and omnipresent, exactly like the self. And then the
Buddhist's whole picture — a stream of fleeting cognitions, each a separate momentary quality — falls
apart. The cognition would not be a momentary flash; it would be the eternal light itself.

The Buddhist tries to escape by saying: "the cognition is not the self's own form; it is a quality of
the self, made by the union with the mind." But this, Abhinavagupta shows, fails too. For what we call
the cognition is the manifestation of the blue and the rest; and if that manifestation is only an
occasional quality, absent when its cause is absent, then the self, apart from it, is simply not
manifesting the blue. The cognition, taken as a separate thing, has no place to stand. Whether you call
it consciousness-form or a quality, it dissolves.

project.text:
**Enjoyment is the meeting of two reflections**

What is it to enjoy — to experience an object? The schools have their answers: the Sāṃkhya makes the
cognition a transformation of matter; the Vaiśeṣika makes it a quality of the self joined to the object
by a mysterious relation called inherence (samavāya). Abhinavagupta cuts through all of this with a
single image: enjoyment is the *union of two reflections* — the reflection of consciousness and the
reflection of the object — meeting in the intellect, and fused by the ego into the one act "I know
this."

Consider what happens when you know the blue. The intellect (buddhi) bears two reflections: the
reflection of consciousness — the light itself, as it is present in the act of knowing — and the
reflection of the blue, the object. The ego (ahaṅkāra) mixes them into the single conceit "I know
this," and that conceit — the two reflections joined, determined by the intellect, resting in the one
consciousness — is the enjoyment. The self, in itself, is not really an enjoyer; it is
consciousness-mere. It is the ego that makes it appear as one who enjoys. And this is not a mere figure
of speech in the loose sense: if it were, then by the infinite division of knowers, the same body could
be dealt with at once as fire and water, as contradictory things, in a single moment — which is absurd.
The enjoyment is real, but real as this union of reflections in the one consciousness.

Now the Vaiśeṣika says: the cognition is a quality of the self, and it is joined to the object by
inherence (samavāya). But Abhinavagupta's point is that the mere *relation* does all the work. If the
cognition-quality is other than the self, then how is it enjoyed? "By inherence," the Vaiśeṣika says.
But then the relation alone is the cause of the enjoyment-form — and that is precisely our point. Here
too there is a relation: the consciousness-reflection, the object-reflection, the ego's mixing, the

project.text:
**Action is the ordered operation, not a thing that moves**

The opponent had offered the self's lordship as the union of knowledge and action. We have seen that
knowledge cannot be a separate thing in his view. Now Abhinavagupta shows that *action* cannot be a
separate thing either. Kārikā 9 makes the point: the action of a body is just the coming-to-be of this
or that place; it is not some hidden cause (the unseen, adṛṣṭa) moving it; and it is not one — for
order does not belong to a single thing.

But wait — if action is not a movement, what is it? The word-knowers, the grammarians, refuse to say
that the body-less self moves. They locate the self's agency only in the union of knowledge, desire,
and effort. So the action that belongs to the self must be defined differently. Its marker,
Abhinavagupta says, is this: the operation of the agent that brings about the fruit — the means,
related to the doer, or inhering in it, or its very self — whose form is such that its parts are
prior-and-later, standing in order. Action is the ordered operation. And the gurus' verses make this
vivid: "as long as the established or un-established is spoken of as the to-be-established, being of
the resting-order-form, it is perceived as that action." The mass of order-born parts, unified by the
mind, is what we call action. "White is whitened" — the whiteness appears as a prior-later order, and
that is the declaration of action. So action is not a thing that moves; it is the ordered self-shaping
of a nature.

And this action is in the self. "He desires, he knows, he strives" — these are the prior-later dharmas
of the one self, perceived in their order; and this ordered operation, Abhinavagupta notes, is accepted
by the very thinkers who hold the self to be the Lord. The guru's words: "such is the will, such the
knowledge, such the action." The will, the knowledge, the action — these are not three separate things
attached to a self; they are the one self's ordered operation, its desir

project.text:
**"Thence the agent too is constructed"**

The Buddhist's attack has been relentless. He has denied the self, denied the cognition, denied the
action. Now he completes it. For what holds all these together — the *relation* between the knower and
the known, between the agent and the act — is itself impossible; and once the relation is gone, "thence
the agent too is constructed." The agent, like everything else, is only a fabrication, a convenient
construction with nothing real behind it.

The kārikā's "thence" gathers a fourfold absence as its reason: the absence of the action, the absence
of the object, the absence of the relation, and the absence of any determination of being in any of
them. And the relation's absence is argued on its own terms. A relation would have to stand *in both*
its terms — in the knower and the known at once. But the two-resting thing cannot be one: what stands
in two cannot be a single thing, any more than the two jars in the two houses are one jar. Moreover,
the established does not expect another — a thing already complete does not reach out for a relation —
and the dependence that a relation would impose is itself unfitting. So the relation is absent; and
with it, the agent that the relation would bind together is only constructed.

Abhinavagupta pauses to make one methodological point, and it is important. The Buddhist thinks he
refutes the relation by a bare non-perception — "I do not see it, so it is not." But a bare
non-perception proves non-being only within a restriction of place and time: "here, now, there is no
jar." It cannot reach the universal non-being of the relation. To do that, one must show a real
contradiction in the opponent's own account — that the very form he ascribes to the relation is
contradicted by another form he ascribes to it. That is a refutation grounded in the thing itself
(prameya-niṣṭha), not a mere failure to perceive.

**The reply: the cognition is self-cognition**

The Buddhist's attack has run its course — the self, the cognition, the action, the relation all
denied, and "thence the agent too is constructed." Now, in the third vimarśa, the established doctrine
replies. And Abhinavagupta's first move is a shrewd concession. "It is true," he begins — and this is
the characteristic gesture of the reflective thinker, granting the opponent what is sound in order to
sharpen what is not. It is true, he says, that the cognition cannot be a separate thing in the way the
Sāṃkhya or the Kāṇāda suppose; that much the Buddhist has rightly seen. But — and here is the turn — the
reason the cognition cannot be a separate thing is precisely because it is *self-cognition*
(svasaṃvid). It is not a quality attached to a self; it is the self's own luminous awareness of itself.
And this self-cognition is the very self the Buddhist thought he had abolished.

Consider memory. When you remember, the prior experience does not stand before you as a new object; it
shines in the single act of the "I" that remembers. The cognition, even in memory, is self-cognition —
it is aware of itself, not of some detached past thing. The Buddhist thought memory freed him from the
self; but memory itself is self-luminous. And if the construction, the determination, were all error —
as the Buddhist would have it — then every determination would fall, and the dealing of the world would
collapse. The Buddhist cannot have it both ways. The memory, the determination, the cognition all
presuppose the self-luminous awareness that is aware of itself in each act.

So the siddhānta's reply rests on the self-luminous dṛk — the seeing that is aware of itself. The "I"
is not constructed; it is that without which no cognition, no memory, no construction could shine at
all. The cognition is self-cognition: it is the light that knows itself, and this light is the self —
the self that the Buddhist denied and Abhinavagupta here restores.

project.text:
**The self-luminous seeing: how the yogin knows another's mind**

We have said the cognition is self-cognition, and the self is self-luminous. But this seems to close
the door on a striking fact — the yogin's knowledge of another's mind. If the self is not an object,
how can the yogin perceive another's cognition with perfect clarity? And if the cognition is
self-luminous only in its own stream, could it not, after all, be manifested by some other cognition?

The answer to the first is that the yogin's knowledge of another is a *perception*, not an inference.
It is the yogipratyakṣa. By the discipline of the yogin — the holding, the meditating, the samādhi —
one comes, in the union with the other, to meditate the non-difference of the self from the other. And
that meditation, following the truth of the thing (for in truth there is unity, and the conceit of
difference is māyā-made), makes the other's cognition shine forth directly, clearly, as a thing seen —
not inferred, not concluded. As the yoga-sūtra says, the knowledge of another's cognition comes by the
saṃyama. The other's passions, too, are manifested in this seeing; but in their very experience the
yogin and the other are one, so the experience shines as self-luminous, not as an object spread before
a detached observer.

And this is the point that matters. The other's cognition, thus seen, is a direct seeing
(sākṣātkāra) — not a conclusion about another stream. And the self that sees, and the self that is
seen, are, in that act, one. So the "being-manifested-by-another" — the picture of one cognition
standing as an object before another — has no place even here. The other knower too is not manifested
by another; he is self-luminous, and in the yogin's perception the two are one.

project.text:
**The determination cannot reach outside**

The Buddhist, having lost the self, the cognition, the action, and the relation, falls back on one
last notion: the *determination* (adhyavasāya) — the act by which, he thinks, the cognition is taken
to establish an external thing. Abhinavagupta now cuts this last thread. The determination, he shows,
cannot establish anything outside.

Consider how the "external" seems to appear. It is, Abhinavagupta says, only the strength of the firm
practice-impression that makes the appearance seem drawn to an external object. From the very first,
the appearance shining in the consciousness and in the determination is taken as external — but only
for the slow-minded, in the illusion and the diseased-eye case. He who knows the cause of the
appearance does not determine its externality at all. The child who cries in astonishment, "the trees
on the far bank rush against the current!" is told: "it is not so — the trees do not rush; it is only
seen so." The manifestation-dharma alone is this. The seeming outwardness is a manner of the seeing,
not a thing established.

And the determination itself, Abhinavagupta presses, is error-form. In every determination — even in
the most ordinary case — there is this error-form, this drawing of the appearance outward. So the
external, which the error-form determination was supposed to establish, has no standing in that very
part: for the part is inert, and an inert thing cannot establish. And in the part that is not inert —
the non-construction, the pure self-experience — there the establishment is not made either, for that
part shines only its own form and its own self-appearance. So the determination's object-establishing
power fails on both sides. The non-erroneous part, the self-experience, is un-divided from the
memory-cognition — it is not a separate thing reaching out to an external — and so it is not
external-natured.

project.text:
**The one who is the whole world: the close of the first volume**

The cognitions, we have seen, are self-luminous and one with the "I." But how, the question arises, do
they not take the form of the "I" when they appear as the objects — the blue, the yellow, the jar? The
answer is that their seeming excess over the "I" — their non-pervasion, their non-eternity, their being
caught in the place and time of the object — is made only by the object-facing condition (upādhi). The
difference of the object, Abhinavagupta says, is a mere conceit (abhimāna), made by the māyā-power; and
even in the state of māyā, the deep un-dividedness of the object from the "I" is un-broken. For māyā is
the Lord's own power — and a power does not cover the power-holder. The māyā cannot hide the Lord's own
form, because it is his own shining. So the whole world, even the seemingly external, is un-divided
from the "I": the one whose body is consciousness, with the inner-made, infinite world-form, possessed
of the knowledge and the rest of the powers.

This is the great vision toward which the volume has been building. The Lord is the one whose body is
the whole world — the inner-made, the outer-form, all of it, un-lost in the least, made by his freedom
and resting in the one knower. The world, counted in the four, the six, the sixteen, the twenty-four,
the thirty-six categories and more, is his body. There is nothing outside the consciousness; the māyā
is his power, not a veil over him.

And the synthesis (anusandhāna) — the act by which the many cognitions are gathered into one — is
itself the consciousness. The objection: "you said the memory's arising is the world's standing; but
here you say 'if the synthesis were not,' and call it consciousness-form — how?" Abhinavagupta answers:
the synthesis of all the knowledges, mutually, *is* the consciousness-tattva. By the co-reference, by

project.text:
**Memory as the Lord's power: how the "I" holds time together**

The jñānādhikāra has established knowledge; now it takes up memory. And here Abhinavagupta makes a
startling claim. The ordinary view — the view of the schools — is that memory is only the revival of an
impression after the experience is gone. When the experience is destroyed, a mere trace remains, and
memory is the stirring of that trace. But Abhinavagupta rejects this. Memory, he insists, is itself a
*knowledge*; and far from being a pale echo of experience, it is the **Lord's own power** — the
un-broken manifestation by which the past and the present are held together in the single "I."

Consider what memory actually does. It brings the previously-experienced object back before the mind;
the object appears, again, in the knower. If memory were only an impression's revival, this would be
inexplicable — for how could a mere trace present an object? The truth is that memory is the un-broken
manifestation of the experienced object: the experience and its object are carried forward into the
memory as one. In memory, the experience does not stand apart as a separate object; it is the very act
of knowing that returns. Even the yogin's knowledge of another, Abhinavagupta notes, does not appear as
a detached object — it is the one awareness continuing. The separation that memory seems to make between
the past cognition and the present one is only a construction (kālpanika), not a real division. And
ultimately, the remembered, the memory, and the rememberer — and by the same token the seen, the seeing,
and the seer — all rest in the one consciousness-essence.

Now the "I" itself. The "aham" shines in two directions at once. As "the seer of the blue" it is turned
inward; but the same "I, thus" is also turned outward toward the blue. The experience is the outward-
facing blue-knowledge. And here is the freedom: by the freedom of the awareness, one first construes,
within, "I would see the blue," and then the bl

project.text:
**The self-luminous cognition: how memory reaches the past, and the yogin reaches the other**

Two puzzles press on the account of memory. The first is the pastness of the past. We remember what
happened yesterday — but how, if the manifestation of consciousness has no touch of time at all? The
answer is that the pastness is not a real quality of the object; it is the *being-previously-manifested*.
The one light, contracting under the limiting conditions of place and time — "yesterday, thirsty, with
that friend, I saw this jar un-ripe" — appears as the past. The manifestation is cut by these upādhis;
and what we call the māyā-word, the realm of ordinary experience, is precisely this contraction of the
light by the conditions. The memory is the re-apprehension of what was previously manifested; and the
cognition of the object, so cut by the past experience, is itself a fresh act of experience. There is
nothing ghostly in memory: it is the one light, narrowed to a past moment, shining again.

The second puzzle is the yogin's perception of another's mind. The yogin is the one who has attained
unity with the supreme knower; for him, all objects are un-cut by time, present in his own self as "I"
or as "I-this." How, then, does one particular appearance arise for him, and with its past-time-
specificity? Here Abhinavagupta gives the key: time is the order of appearing and not-appearing. The
body, flashing and fading moment by moment, is what gives the endless difference of time. Those who
take the body as the knower are bound in the chain of time, and can never see past or future. But the
yogin, by the teaching and the sustained meditation, thins the body — and then the other's cognition
shines in its own place.

And this leads to the deepest point: the nature of cognition itself. The cognition is
self-cognition (svasaṃvitti). Its own nature — that which never deviates, the marker neither over- nor
under-pervading — is to be self-luminous, the own-awareness that distingui

project.text:
**The self-luminous cognition is never the object of another**

We have seen that the yogin, by the purity and the un-opposed spreading of his cognition, knows
another's cognition. But this draws a sharp objection from the epistemologist. "Even granting that," he
says, "a cognition can never be the *object* of another cognition. For how can one awareness be known
by a second? The two would have to stand in the relation of object and holder — and between two
cognitions no such relation is possible."

Abhinavagupta takes this seriously and analyzes what "being an object" really means. A thing is an
object of a cognition when the awareness *assimilates its form* — when it takes on the form of the
thing, as the blue-awareness takes on the blue. This assimilation is the sārūpya, the conformity of the
cognition to its object. And it requires that the object be *both* like and unlike the cognition: in
total identity the thing would be the cognition itself, and in total difference there would be nothing
to assimilate. Now here is the crux. A cognition has no such difference from another cognition. The
difference of place, time, and form is absent between two awarenesses; the difference that comes from
the object (the blue) is not the param-essence of the cognition; and though the object-part — the blue
— or the intent-part — the passion — can be an object by a separate manifestation, the *awareness-part*
itself can never be an object at all. An awareness cannot be spread before itself as a thing to be
grasped.

Abhinavagupta makes this vivid with two mirrors. Two mirrors can reflect one another, each bearing the
other's image — because their forms, being of place and time, are genuinely distinct. But two
cognitions are not like that. Their form is not the place-time form of things; it is the self-luminous
awareness, which has nothing in it to be set over against another awareness. So the object-holder
relation between two cognitions is impossible: there is no perception of

project.text:
**The knowledge-power: manifestation as the very form of things**

We have examined memory and the construction. But both presuppose something deeper — the
knowledge-power (jñānaśakti), the capacity by which anything at all is known. And here Abhinavagupta
makes the central claim of this vimarśa: **the manifestation is the very form of the objects.** The
things of the world are not hidden realities that a light shines upon from outside; their being *is*
their being-manifested. To know a thing is not to touch something beyond the light; it is to be the
light in which that thing appears.

Consider the present beings. As they manifest, they manifest "as the outer-self" — the inner
standing-alone of consciousness, pouring itself out as the external world. The jar before you is not a
thing outside that your mind then copies; it is the inner light, standing as the outer form. Memory and
the construction, for their part, do not present a common object as something separate and distinct; and
even in perception, the object does not exceed the experience that reveals it. The thing is not more
than its being-manifested.

Now the Vijñānavādin, the Buddhist idealist, agrees that the object is not outside — but he draws the
wrong conclusion. He concludes that there is no object at all, only the inner cognition with its blue
form. Abhinavagupta replies that this does not follow. The cognition's inner blue-form is a
*reflection*; and a reflection expects a ground that it reflects — as a mirror-image expects the thing
before the mirror. So the inner blue-form, being a reflection, points to an identical ground that
produces it. This is the inference of the object: not as a thing hidden beyond all experience, but as
the ground whose reflection the blue-form is. Even as the sense-organ is inferred from the perception
it causes, so the object is inferred as the cause of its manifestation. The object is real — but its
reality is to be the ground of the manifestation, not a bare thing bey

project.text:
**How the external object is inferred and confirmed**

The Vijñānavādin grants that the cognition is self-luminous, but he presses on its inner form. "The
cognition's blue-form," he says, "is a reflection (pratibimba); and a reflection demands a ground that
produces it (the arpaka). So the external object is inferred." But then the classic objection follows:
how can you infer an external object that is never perceived? An inference rests on a pervasion grasped
in perception — and the external is never perceived at all.

Abhinavagupta answers with the sense-organ analogy. The sense-organ itself is never perceived — yet we
infer it as the cause of the perceptions it produces. The eye is inferred from the seeing, not seen.
So too the external object: though never perceived as an object, it is inferred as the cause of its
cognition. And the mechanism is the sārūpya, the conformity: the inner blue-form, with all its
place-and-time variety, un-lost, points to its ground — the object similar to it. The determination "I
see this object" arises from this conformity, and it is not a bare error, like the shell-silver in the
grasped shell.

For here is the crucial point, and Abhinavagupta states it boldly: even this determination, though it
begins as error — the drawing of the inner form outward — is, by its bond to the thing, a *valid means*.
As the rule has it, "even the error, being a relation, is a pramā." The determination, by the strength
of the seeing, takes the form "I see" and enlists the perception as the object's helper — as a minister
moves a king who has been won over. So the external object, thus determined and confirmed, is
perceived (pratyakṣa-gṛhīta).

And what, then, is the inference's own work? It is the sasaṃvāda — the agreement. The inference
establishes that the root-cause, the ground of the forms (the arpaka), is the object similar to the
form. This is its operation: not to create the object, but to confirm that the ground of the cognition's

project.text:
**You cannot infer another's mind — and you do not need the external object**

The Buddhist hopes to escape by inferring *another's* mind. He thinks: from Maitra's speech, from his
uttered words and gestures, one can infer what is going on in his mind — the other stream. Abhinavagupta
shows this inference cannot work, and he does it with a precise analogy.

Suppose you want to infer the fire *in the sandalwood* from the smoke. If you set aside the
sandalwood's fragrance — the very thing that marks this smoke as coming from sandalwood — then you
establish only fire in general, not the sandalwood-fire. The distinction must be accepted; without it
the desired conclusion is not reached. But to infer another's mind, you would need exactly such a
further distinction — the "being-gone-to-the-other," the fact that this utterance belongs to Maitra and
not to you. And that distinction cannot be inferred from the mere utterance. The utterance could belong
to anything; nothing in it, by itself, says "this is Maitra's intent, this is another's mind."

And the "being-gone-to-the-other," Abhinavagupta argues, is not like the sandalwood-fragrance, a
further distinguishing mark resting apart from the thing. It is a different kind of thing entirely. To
press the point, he notes that if every additional feature were a "further distinction," then "cow" and
"speckled" would both be separate things, and the statement "the cow is the speckled" would fail. But
that statement holds; so a real further-distinction is something that rests apart from the thing, and
the "being-gone-to-the-other" does not rest apart from the mere utterance in the way that would make it
inferable.

Moreover — and this is the decisive point — only the *aimed* action (samīhitā) is the wish's effect.
A wish produces the action it intends, not a mere utterance or gesture that could be aimed at anything.
So from Maitra's mere utterance one cannot infer his wish, since the utterance does not reveal which
aim it serves.
